diagrams.title: S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism of CH<sub>3</sub>Cl with OH<sup>−</sup>
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three stages left to right. Stage 1: the carbon of CH<sub>3</sub>Cl with Cl on the right and the three hydrogens fanned to the left, and HO<sup>−</sup> approaching from the left (opposite side to Cl) with a curved arrow from the oxygen lone pair to carbon and another from the C–Cl bond onto Cl. Stage 2, in square brackets with a double-dagger sign: the transition state with the three hydrogens in one plane and dotted bonds HO···C···Cl carrying δ− on both O and Cl. Stage 3: CH<sub>3</sub>OH with the hydrogens now fanned to the right, plus Cl<sup>−</sup>. Label 'backside attack', 'transition state' and 'inversion of configuration'.

diagrams.title: S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr with OH<sup>−</sup>
diagrams.how_to_draw: Two steps one under the other. Step 1 (label 'slow, rate determining'): (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Br with a curved arrow from the C–Br bond to Br, an equilibrium arrow, and the planar (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> carbocation drawn as a trigonal planar carbon plus Br<sup>−</sup>. Step 2 (label 'fast'): OH<sup>−</sup> attacking the carbocation to give (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH. Add a note that the nucleophile can attack the planar carbocation from either face, so an optically active halide gives a racemic mixture.

diagrams.title: Resonance structures of chlorobenzene
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw five structures joined by double-headed arrows. The first is ordinary chlorobenzene with two lone pairs on Cl. In the second, a lone pair from Cl forms C=Cl<sup>+</sup> and the ring carries a negative charge on the ortho carbon. Move the negative charge to the para carbon in the third and to the other ortho carbon in the fourth, then back to neutral chlorobenzene in the fifth. Write under it: 'partial double-bond character of C–Cl; electron density at ortho and para positions'. The same drawing is used for low reactivity to nucleophiles and for o/p-direction in electrophilic substitution.

diagrams.title: Enantiomers of 2-chlorobutane (chirality)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a vertical dashed line for the mirror. On the left draw C-2 as a tetrahedral carbon with H (wedge), Cl (dash), CH<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> as the four groups. On the right draw its mirror image with the wedge and dash positions swapped. Label the two forms as enantiomers, mark the stereocentre with an asterisk, and note that they are non-superimposable and rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions. For contrast, a small drawing of 2-chloropropane with two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups shows why it is achiral.

diagrams.title: Effect of nitro groups on hydrolysis of chlorobenzene
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw four benzene rings with Cl at the top: plain chlorobenzene, 4-nitro, 2,4-dinitro and 2,4,6-trinitro. Under each write the condition needed to replace Cl by OH: NaOH 623 K 300 atm; 15% NaOH 443 K; 15% NaOH 368 K; warm water. Add an arrow showing 'ease of nucleophilic substitution increases' left to right, and a footnote that a meta-nitro group has no effect.

ncert_questions.q: Give the IUPAC names of the following compounds: (i) CH<sub>3</sub>CH(Cl)CH(Br)CH<sub>3</sub> (ii) CHF<sub>2</sub>CBrClF (iii) ClCH<sub>2</sub>C≡CCH<sub>2</sub>Br (iv) (CCl<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCl (v) CH<sub>3</sub>C(p-ClC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH(Br)CH<sub>3</sub> (vi) (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCH=C(Cl)C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>I-p
ncert_questions.a:
(i) 2-Bromo-3-chlorobutane (bromo comes first alphabetically, so it gets the lower locant).

(ii) 1-Bromo-1-chloro-1,2,2-trifluoroethane.

(iii) 1-Bromo-4-chlorobut-2-yne.

(iv) 2-(Trichloromethyl)-1,1,1,2,3,3,3-heptachloropropane.

(v) 2-Bromo-3,3-bis(4-chlorophenyl)butane.

(vi) 1-Chloro-1-(4-iodophenyl)-3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene.

Show the chain numbering on the structure if you draw it; alphabetical order decides ties.

ncert_questions.q: Which one of the following has the highest dipole moment? (i) CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> (ii) CHCl<sub>3</sub> (iii) CCl<sub>4</sub>
ncert_questions.a: CH2Cl2 (dichloromethane) has the highest dipole moment. In CCl4 the four C–Cl dipoles are arranged tetrahedrally and cancel completely, so μ = 0. In CHCl3 the resultant of two C–Cl dipoles opposes the third C–Cl dipole, so the net moment is small (about 1.08 D). In CH2Cl2 the resultant of the two C–Cl dipoles is reinforced by the resultant of the two C–H dipoles, giving the largest net moment (about 1.60 D). Order: CH2Cl2 > CHCl3 > CCl4.

ncert_questions.q: A hydrocarbon C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> does not react with chlorine in the dark but gives a single monochloro compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Cl in bright sunlight. Identify the hydrocarbon.
ncert_questions.a: C5H10 fits either an alkene or a cycloalkane. An alkene would add chlorine even in the dark, so the compound is saturated: it is a cycloalkane. Of the cycloalkanes with this formula, only cyclopentane has all ten hydrogens equivalent, so free-radical substitution in sunlight gives a single product, chlorocyclopentane. The hydrocarbon is cyclopentane.

ncert_questions.q: Write the isomers of the compound having formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br.
ncert_questions.a: Four isomers: (i) CH3CH2CH2CH2Br, 1-bromobutane (1°); (ii) CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3, 2-bromobutane (2°, chiral); (iii) (CH3)2CHCH2Br, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (1°); (iv) (CH3)3CBr, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (3°). The first two are chain isomers of the last two, and each pair are position isomers of each other.

ncert_questions.q: Write the equations for the preparation of 1-iodobutane from (i) 1-butanol (ii) 1-chlorobutane (iii) but-1-ene.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) CH3CH2CH2CH2OH + KI + H3PO4 → CH3CH2CH2CH2I + KH2PO4 + H2O (HI generated in situ; alternatively red P + I2).

(ii) Finkelstein reaction: CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl + NaI → CH3CH2CH2CH2I + NaCl↓ (dry acetone, heat).

(iii) Markovnikov addition of HI: CH3CH2CH=CH2 + HI → CH3CH2CH(I)CH3 gives 2-iodobutane, not the target. So first add HBr in the presence of peroxide to get 1-bromobutane (anti-Markovnikov), then do the Finkelstein reaction with NaI in acetone to get 1-iodobutane. (HI itself shows no peroxide effect.)

ncert_questions.q: What are ambident nucleophiles? Explain with an example.
ncert_questions.a: Ambident nucleophiles are nucleophiles that have two nucleophilic centres and can attack through either of them. Cyanide ion is a resonance hybrid of −:C≡N and :C=N−, so it can bond through carbon or nitrogen. With ionic KCN the attack is through carbon and an alkyl cyanide (nitrile) forms, because the C–C bond is stronger than the C–N bond; with covalent AgCN the carbon is bonded to silver, so nitrogen attacks and the isocyanide forms: CH3CH2Br + KCN → CH3CH2CN, but CH3CH2Br + AgCN → CH3CH2NC. Nitrite ion behaves similarly: KNO2 gives the alkyl nitrite R–O–N=O, AgNO2 gives the nitroalkane R–NO2.

ncert_questions.q: Which compound in each of the following pairs will react faster in S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction with OH<sup>−</sup>? (i) CH<sub>3</sub>Br or CH<sub>3</sub>I (ii) (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCl or CH<sub>3</sub>Cl
ncert_questions.a:
(i) CH3I reacts faster. I− is a better leaving group than Br− because the C–I bond is longer and weaker (bond enthalpy 234 against 293 kJ mol−1) and iodide is a larger, more stable ion.

(ii) CH3Cl reacts faster. SN2 needs backside attack on the carbon; in (CH3)3CCl the three methyl groups crowd the carbon and hinder the nucleophile, so the tertiary halide is the least reactive by SN2 (it prefers SN1).

ncert_questions.q: Predict all the alkenes that would be formed by dehydrohalogenation of the following halides with sodium ethoxide in ethanol and identify the major alkene: (i) 1-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexane (ii) 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane (iii) 2,2,3-Trimethyl-3-bromopentane.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) β-Hydrogens are on the ring CH2 groups and on the CH3. Products: 1-methylcyclohexene (major; trisubstituted double bond inside the ring) and methylenecyclohexane (minor; disubstituted, exocyclic).

(ii) (CH3)2C(Cl)CH2CH3 loses H from C-1 or C-3. Products: 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3 (major, trisubstituted), and 2-methylbut-1-ene, CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3 (minor, disubstituted).

(iii) (CH3)3C–C(Br)(CH3)–CH2CH3 has β-hydrogens on the CH3 and on the CH2 (the tert-butyl carbon has none). Products: 3,4,4-trimethylpent-2-ene, CH3CH=C(CH3)C(CH3)3 (major, trisubstituted), and 2-ethyl-3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene, CH2=C(C2H5)C(CH3)3 (minor). In each case Saytzeff's rule picks the more substituted alkene as major.

ncert_questions.q: Explain why (i) the dipole moment of chlorobenzene is lower than that of cyclohexyl chloride; (ii) alkyl halides, though polar, are immiscible with water; (iii) Grignard reagents should be prepared under anhydrous conditions.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) In chlorobenzene the carbon bonded to Cl is sp2 hybridised and so more electronegative than the sp3 carbon of cyclohexyl chloride; it pulls electron density back from Cl and the C–Cl bond is less polar. Also, resonance delocalises the lone pairs of Cl into the ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character and reducing the charge separation. Both lower the dipole moment.

(ii) For an alkyl halide to dissolve, the hydrogen bonds between water molecules and the dipole-dipole attractions between alkyl halide molecules must be broken. The new attractions between alkyl halide and water are weaker than the hydrogen bonds broken, so the energy is not recovered and the two liquids do not mix.

(iii) Grignard reagents are very reactive towards any compound with an acidic hydrogen; even the traces of water in the solvent decompose them: RMgX + H2O → RH + Mg(OH)X. Hence they are prepared in dry ether under anhydrous conditions.

ncert_questions.q: Write the mechanism of the following reaction: n-BuBr + KCN → n-BuCN (in ethanol–water).
ncert_questions.a:
1-Bromobutane is a primary halide, so the reaction goes by the SN2 mechanism in one step. KCN ionises to give CN−, an ambident nucleophile that attacks through carbon because the C–C bond that forms is stronger than a C–N bond.

Mechanism: the cyanide carbon attacks C-1 of CH3CH2CH2CH2Br from the side opposite to bromine. A transition state forms in which carbon is partially bonded to both CN and Br, with the two hydrogens and the propyl group in one plane: [NC···CH2(C3H7)···Br]δ−. The C–Br bond breaks as the C–C bond forms, bromide leaves, and the configuration at carbon inverts: NC− + CH3CH2CH2CH2Br → CH3CH2CH2CH2CN + Br−. Rate = k[n-BuBr][CN−], second order.

ncert_questions.q: Arrange the compounds of each set in order of reactivity towards S<sub>N</sub>2 displacement: (i) 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-Bromopentane, 2-Bromopentane (ii) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane, 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 3-Bromo-2-methylbutane (iii) 1-Bromobutane, 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane, 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane.
ncert_questions.a:
SN2 is slowed by crowding around the carbon carrying the halogen, so 1° > 2° > 3°, and among primary halides the one with branching nearer the C–Br carbon is slower.

(i) 1-Bromopentane (1°) > 2-bromopentane (2°) > 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (3°).

(ii) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane (1°) > 3-bromo-2-methylbutane (2°) > 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (3°).

(iii) All are primary, so compare the branching: 1-bromobutane (no branch) > 1-bromo-3-methylbutane (branch at C-3) > 1-bromo-2-methylbutane (branch at C-2) > 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (two branches at C-2, most hindered).

ncert_questions.q: p-Dichlorobenzene has higher melting point and lower solubility than those of o- and m-isomers. Discuss.
ncert_questions.a: The para isomer is symmetrical, so its molecules pack closely and fit well into the crystal lattice. The intermolecular forces in the solid are therefore stronger than in the less symmetrical ortho and meta isomers. More energy is needed to break the lattice, so the melting point is higher; and the solvent must also supply more energy to pull the molecules out of the lattice, so the solubility is lower.

ncert_questions.q: The treatment of alkyl chlorides with aqueous KOH leads to the formation of alcohols but in the presence of alcoholic KOH, alkenes are major products. Explain.
ncert_questions.a:
In aqueous solution KOH is fully ionised and gives OH− ions, which are strong nucleophiles. They attack the electron-deficient carbon of C–Cl and displace Cl− (substitution), so an alcohol forms: RCH2CH2Cl + KOH(aq) → RCH2CH2OH + KCl.

In alcoholic solution KOH reacts with ethanol to give ethoxide ions, C2H5O−, which are stronger bases than nucleophiles and also bulkier. They prefer to abstract a β-hydrogen, and the halide leaves from the α-carbon (β-elimination), giving the alkene: RCH2CH2Cl + KOH(alc.) → RCH=CH2 + KCl + H2O. Also, water being a better solvating solvent stabilises the transition state of substitution, while alcohol does not.

ncert_questions.q: Primary alkyl halide C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br (a) reacted with alcoholic KOH to give compound (b). Compound (b) is reacted with HBr to give (c) which is an isomer of (a). When (a) is reacted with sodium metal it gives compound (d), C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>, which is different from the compound formed when n-butyl bromide is reacted with sodium. Give the structural formula of (a) and write the equations for all the reactions.
ncert_questions.a:
There are two primary isomers of C4H9Br: 1-bromobutane and 1-bromo-2-methylpropane. Since (d) differs from n-octane (the Wurtz product of n-butyl bromide), (a) must be 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (isobutyl bromide), (CH3)2CHCH2Br.

(a) → (b): (CH3)2CHCH2Br + KOH (alc.) → (CH3)2C=CH2 (2-methylpropene) + KBr + H2O.

(b) → (c): (CH3)2C=CH2 + HBr → (CH3)3CBr, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (Markovnikov addition), a positional isomer of (a).

(a) → (d): 2(CH3)2CHCH2Br + 2Na → (CH3)2CHCH2CH2CH(CH3)2 (2,5-dimethylhexane) + 2NaBr, in dry ether (Wurtz reaction). n-Butyl bromide would give CH3(CH2)6CH3, n-octane, a different compound.

ncert_questions.q: What happens when (i) n-butyl chloride is treated with alcoholic KOH, (ii) bromobenzene is treated with Mg in the presence of dry ether, (iii) chlorobenzene is subjected to hydrolysis, (iv) ethyl chloride is treated with aqueous KOH, (v) methyl bromide is treated with sodium in the presence of dry ether, (vi) methyl chloride is treated with KCN?
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Dehydrohalogenation gives but-1-ene: CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl + KOH (alc.) → CH3CH2CH=CH2 + KCl + H2O.

(ii) Phenylmagnesium bromide, a Grignard reagent, forms: C6H5Br + Mg → C6H5MgBr.

(iii) Chlorobenzene is not hydrolysed under ordinary conditions; with NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm it gives sodium phenoxide, which on acidification gives phenol: C6H5Cl + NaOH → C6H5ONa → C6H5OH.

(iv) Substitution gives ethanol: C2H5Cl + KOH (aq) → C2H5OH + KCl.

(v) Wurtz reaction gives ethane: 2CH3Br + 2Na → CH3CH3 + 2NaBr.

(vi) Ethanenitrile (methyl cyanide) forms: CH3Cl + KCN → CH3CN + KCl.

ncert_questions.q: Among the isomeric alkanes of molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, identify the one that on photochemical chlorination yields (i) a single monochloride (ii) three isomeric monochlorides (iii) four isomeric monochlorides.
ncert_questions.a:
C5H12 has three isomers: n-pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

(i) A single monochloride: 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane), C(CH3)4. All twelve hydrogens are equivalent, so only 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane forms.

(ii) Three isomeric monochlorides: n-pentane, CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3, which has three sets of equivalent hydrogens (C-1/C-5, C-2/C-4, C-3), giving 1-chloro-, 2-chloro- and 3-chloropentane.

(iii) Four isomeric monochlorides: 2-methylbutane, (CH3)2CHCH2CH3, which has four sets of hydrogens, giving 1-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-3-methylbutane and 1-chloro-3-methylbutane.

ncert_questions.q: Arrange each set of compounds in order of increasing boiling points: (i) Bromomethane, bromoform, chloromethane, dibromomethane (ii) 1-Chloropropane, isopropyl chloride, 1-chlorobutane.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Boiling point rises with the mass and number of halogen atoms, because van der Waals forces get stronger: chloromethane < bromomethane < dibromomethane < bromoform.

(ii) Boiling point rises with the number of carbons and falls with branching: isopropyl chloride (branched, C3) < 1-chloropropane (straight, C3) < 1-chlorobutane (C4).

pyq.q: Which of the following is an example of a vic-dihalide?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: A vicinal dihalide has the two halogens on adjacent carbons; 1,2-dichloroethane (ethylene dichloride) is the example. Ethylidene chloride, CH<sub>3</sub>CHCl<sub>2</sub>, is a gem-dihalide; dichloromethane has both Cl on one carbon; allyl chloride is a monohalide.

pyq.q: Which of the following alkyl halides will undergo S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction most readily?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: All four give the same tertiary carbocation, so the rate is decided by the leaving group. C–I is the longest and weakest bond and I<sup>−</sup> the best leaving group, so the iodide ionises fastest: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

pyq.q: Which of the following molecules is chiral?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Only 2-bromobutane has a carbon (C-2) bonded to four different groups: H, Br, CH<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>. The others have at least two identical groups on every carbon.

pyq.q: The reaction of ethyl bromide with NaI in dry acetone to give ethyl iodide is called
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Halogen exchange with NaI in dry acetone is the Finkelstein reaction; NaBr precipitates in acetone and drives it forward. Swarts uses metal fluorides to make alkyl fluorides.

pyq.q: Which of the following has the highest boiling point?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: For the same alkyl group the boiling point rises with the size and mass of the halogen (RI > RBr > RCl), and the branched isopropyl bromide boils below 1-bromopropane. 1-Iodopropane is the highest.

pyq.q: Ethyl bromide on treatment with AgCN gives mainly
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: AgCN is covalent, so the carbon of CN is bonded to silver and the free nitrogen attacks the alkyl halide, giving ethyl isocyanide, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NC. Ionic KCN would give propanenitrile, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CN.

pyq.q: Chlorobenzene on heating with aqueous NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm followed by acidification gives
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: This is the Dow's process: under these severe conditions OH<sup>−</sup> replaces Cl to give sodium phenoxide, which on acidification gives phenol. The harsh conditions reflect the partial double-bond character of the C–Cl bond.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Chlorobenzene is less reactive than chloroethane towards nucleophilic substitution. Reason (R): The C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene acquires partial double-bond character due to resonance.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Resonance delocalises the chlorine lone pair into the ring, making the C–Cl bond shorter, stronger and harder to break, which is exactly why haloarenes resist nucleophilic substitution.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Tert-butyl bromide undergoes hydrolysis by the S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism. Reason (R): The tert-butyl carbocation is stabilised by three electron-releasing methyl groups.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: S<sub>N</sub>1 proceeds through a carbocation; the stability of the tertiary carbocation (hyperconjugation and +I effect of three methyl groups) makes the slow ionisation step feasible, so the tertiary halide reacts by S<sub>N</sub>1.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Addition of HBr to propene in the presence of peroxide gives 1-bromopropane. Reason (R): HCl and HI also show the peroxide effect.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Peroxide causes anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr, so 1-bromopropane forms (A true). The peroxide effect is shown only by HBr, not by HCl or HI (R false).

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Aryl halides cannot be prepared by replacing the hydroxyl group of phenol by halogen using HX or PX<sub>3</sub>. Reason (R): The C–O bond in phenol has partial double-bond character and is not easily broken.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Resonance between the oxygen lone pair and the ring gives the phenolic C–O bond partial double-bond character, so unlike alcohols, phenols do not give aryl halides with HX or phosphorus halides.

pyq.q: Why is sulphuric acid not used during the reaction of alcohols with KI?
pyq.answer: Concentrated H2SO4 is a strong oxidising agent. The HI produced in situ from KI is a reducing agent and is oxidised by H2SO4 to I2 (2HI + H2SO4 → I2 + SO2 + 2H2O), so it is no longer available to convert the alcohol into the alkyl iodide. Non-oxidising 95% orthophosphoric acid is used instead. (1 mark for the oxidising nature, 1 for HI → I2 and the alternative acid.)

pyq.q: Give reasons: (i) Alkyl halides, though polar, are immiscible with water. (ii) Grignard reagents should be prepared under anhydrous conditions.
pyq.answer:
(i) To dissolve, the hydrogen bonds between water molecules and the dipole-dipole forces between alkyl halide molecules must be broken. The new attractions between alkyl halide and water are weaker than the hydrogen bonds that would be lost, so the energy is not recovered and the liquids stay separate. (1 mark)

(ii) Grignard reagents react with any compound that has an acidic hydrogen, and water is enough: RMgX + H2O → R–H + Mg(OH)X. Any moisture would destroy the reagent, so it is made in dry ether under anhydrous conditions. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Out of S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2, which reaction occurs with (i) inversion of configuration (ii) racemisation? Give reason in each case.
pyq.answer:
(i) SN2. The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving group in a single step, so the three other groups flip over like an umbrella and the product has the inverted configuration. (1 mark)

(ii) SN1. The intermediate carbocation is planar (sp2), so the nucleophile can attack from either face with equal probability, giving equal amounts of the two enantiomers, a racemic mixture. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Write the structure of the major product formed when (i) 2-bromopentane is heated with alcoholic KOH; (ii) chlorobenzene is treated with CH<sub>3</sub>Cl in the presence of anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub>.
pyq.answer:
(i) Dehydrohalogenation; by Saytzeff's rule the more substituted alkene is major: pent-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH2CH3 (pent-1-ene is minor). (1 mark)

(ii) Friedel-Crafts alkylation; chlorine is ortho/para-directing and the para product predominates: 4-chlorotoluene (1-chloro-4-methylbenzene), with a little 2-chlorotoluene. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Which one in each pair will react faster and why? (i) S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl or C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH(Cl)C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> (ii) S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction: 1-bromobutane or 2-bromobutane
pyq.answer:
(i) C6H5CH(Cl)C6H5 reacts faster by SN1. Its carbocation, (C6H5)2CH+, is stabilised by resonance with two phenyl rings, whereas the benzyl cation has only one. (1 mark)

(ii) 1-Bromobutane reacts faster by SN2. It is a primary halide, so the carbon is less hindered and the nucleophile can attack from the back side more easily than at the secondary carbon of 2-bromobutane. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Explain why haloarenes are much less reactive than haloalkanes towards nucleophilic substitution reactions.
pyq.answer:
Any three of the following, with the resonance structures of chlorobenzene drawn for full credit:

  1. Resonance effect: the lone pairs on chlorine are delocalised into the benzene ring, so the C–Cl bond acquires partial double-bond character. It is shorter (169 pm against 177 pm) and stronger than in haloalkanes and is difficult to break.
  2. Hybridisation: in haloarenes the halogen is attached to an sp2 carbon, which has more s-character and is more electronegative than the sp3 carbon of haloalkanes; it holds the bonding pair more tightly, shortening and strengthening the bond.
  3. Instability of phenyl cation: an SN1 route would require a phenyl cation, which is not stabilised by resonance (the empty orbital is perpendicular to the π system), so it does not form.
  4. Repulsion: the electron-rich aromatic ring repels the approaching electron-rich nucleophile.

Hence chlorobenzene needs 623 K and 300 atm with NaOH to give phenol, while chloroethane is hydrolysed by warm aqueous KOH.

pyq.q: Write the mechanism of the hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide by aqueous KOH. What happens to an optically active alkyl halide in such a reaction?
pyq.answer:
Tertiary halides react by SN1 in two steps.

Step 1 (slow, rate determining): the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, helped by the polar protic solvent, to give the planar tert-butyl carbocation and Br−: (CH3)3C–Br → (CH3)3C+ + Br−. The carbocation is stabilised by the +I effect and hyperconjugation of three methyl groups.

Step 2 (fast): the hydroxide ion attacks the carbocation: (CH3)3C+ + OH− → (CH3)3C–OH. Rate = k[(CH3)3CBr], first order, independent of [OH−]. (2 marks for the two steps with the rate law)

Stereochemistry: the carbocation is sp2 and planar, so OH− can bond from either face with equal probability. An optically active halide therefore gives equal amounts of the two enantiomeric alcohols, a racemic mixture, and the product is optically inactive (racemisation). (1 mark)

pyq.q: What happens when (i) ethyl chloride is treated with AgNO<sub>2</sub>, (ii) chlorobenzene is treated with Cl<sub>2</sub> in the presence of FeCl<sub>3</sub>, (iii) methyl bromide is treated with KCN followed by treatment with H<sub>2</sub>/Ni? Write the chemical equations.
pyq.answer:
(i) AgNO2 is covalent, so nitrogen attacks and nitroethane forms: C2H5Cl + AgNO2 → C2H5NO2 + AgCl. (With KNO2 the product would be ethyl nitrite, C2H5ONO.)

(ii) Electrophilic substitution; Cl is ortho/para-directing, so 1,4-dichlorobenzene (major) and 1,2-dichlorobenzene (minor) form: C6H5Cl + Cl2 → C6H4Cl2 + HCl (anhydrous FeCl3).

(iii) KCN gives ethanenitrile, which is then reduced to ethanamine: CH3Br + KCN → CH3CN + KBr; CH3CN + 2H2 → CH3CH2NH2 (Ni). Note that the chain grows by one carbon, a step used in conversions.

pyq.q: Arrange the following in the order indicated and give one reason for each: (i) Increasing boiling point: 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, 1-chloropropane. (ii) Increasing reactivity towards S<sub>N</sub>2: CH<sub>3</sub>Br, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHBr, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br. (iii) Increasing ease of nucleophilic substitution: chlorobenzene, 4-nitrochlorobenzene, 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene.
pyq.answer:
(i) 1-Chloropropane < 2-bromo-2-methylpropane < 1-chlorobutane < 1-bromobutane. Boiling point rises with the number of carbons and with the mass of the halogen, and falls with branching; the tertiary bromide is compact, so despite bromine it boils below 1-chlorobutane (about 346 K against 351 K), while 1-bromobutane (about 375 K) is highest. (1 mark)

(ii) (CH3)2CHBr < CH3CH2Br < CH3Br. SN2 needs backside attack, and steric hindrance around the carbon increases from methyl to primary to secondary. (1 mark)

(iii) Chlorobenzene < 4-nitrochlorobenzene < 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene. Electron-withdrawing nitro groups at ortho/para positions delocalise the negative charge of the intermediate carbanion and make substitution easier; the conditions fall from 623 K/300 atm to 443 K to 368 K. (1 mark)

pyq.q: An alkyl halide (A), C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br, is optically active. On treatment with alcoholic KOH it gives (B), which on ozonolysis gives two aldehydes. On treatment with aqueous KOH, (A) gives (C), an optically active alcohol. Identify (A), (B) and (C) and write the reactions.
pyq.answer:
(A) is optically active, so it must contain a chiral carbon: of the four isomers of C4H9Br only 2-bromobutane, CH3CH(Br)CH2CH3, has one. (1 mark)

(A) + KOH (alc.) → (B): by Saytzeff's rule the major alkene is but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3. Ozonolysis of but-2-ene gives two molecules of ethanal, CH3CHO; a symmetrical internal alkene gives 'two aldehydes' in the sense of two aldehyde molecules, which fits. (1 mark)

(A) + KOH (aq) → (C): substitution gives butan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, which is optically active because C-2 still carries four different groups. Since a secondary halide reacts largely by SN2, the alcohol has the inverted configuration. (1 mark)

pyq.q: (a) Describe the S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism with the example of chloromethane and hydroxide ion, including the rate law and the stereochemical outcome. (b) Compare S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanisms on any three points. (c) Which of CH<sub>3</sub>Cl, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl and (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCl would react fastest by S<sub>N</sub>1, and why?
pyq.answer:
(a) CH3Cl + OH− → CH3OH + Cl−. The reaction is second order: rate = k[CH3Cl][OH−], so both species take part in the single rate-determining step. The hydroxide ion attacks the carbon from the side opposite to chlorine. In the transition state carbon is partially bonded to both OH and Cl, with the three hydrogens in a plane perpendicular to the O···C···Cl line; the negative charge is shared between O and Cl. As the C–O bond forms the C–Cl bond breaks and chloride leaves. The three hydrogens swing over like an umbrella turned inside out, so if the carbon is a stereocentre the product has the inverted configuration (Walden inversion). Reactivity: CH3X > 1° > 2° > 3°, because bulky groups hinder the backside attack. (2 marks: mechanism with transition state, rate law and inversion)

(b) SN1: two steps via a carbocation; rate = k[RX], first order; reactivity 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3X; racemisation; favoured by polar protic solvents and weak nucleophiles. SN2: one step via a transition state; rate = k[RX][Nu−], second order; reactivity CH3X > 1° > 2° > 3°; inversion; favoured by strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents. (2 marks for any three contrasts)

(c) (CH3)3CCl reacts fastest by SN1. The rate depends on the stability of the carbocation formed in the slow step, and the tertiary carbocation is the most stable because of the +I effect and hyperconjugation of three methyl groups. Order: (CH3)3CCl > (CH3)2CHCl > CH3Cl. (1 mark)

pyq.q: How will you bring about the following conversions? Write the reactions. (i) Benzene to biphenyl (ii) Propene to 1-nitropropane (iii) Ethanol to but-1-yne (iv) Aniline to chlorobenzene (v) Toluene to benzyl alcohol
pyq.answer:
(i) Chlorinate, then Fittig: C6H6 + Cl2 → C6H5Cl (anhydrous FeCl3); 2C6H5Cl + 2Na → C6H5–C6H5 + 2NaCl (dry ether). (1 mark)

(ii) Anti-Markovnikov HBr, then AgNO2: CH3CH=CH2 + HBr → CH3CH2CH2Br (peroxide); CH3CH2CH2Br + AgNO2 → CH3CH2CH2NO2 + AgBr. Without peroxide you would get 2-bromopropane and hence 2-nitropropane. (1 mark)

(iii) Make ethyl bromide and couple it with sodium acetylide: C2H5OH + HBr → C2H5Br + H2O; separately, ethanol → ethyl bromide → (alc. KOH) ethene → (Br2) 1,2-dibromoethane → (NaNH2) ethyne → (NaNH2) sodium acetylide, HC≡C−Na+; then HC≡CNa + C2H5Br → HC≡C–CH2CH3 (but-1-yne) + NaBr. (1 mark)

(iv) Diazotise, then Sandmeyer: C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl → C6H5N2+Cl− + NaCl + 2H2O (273–278 K); C6H5N2+Cl− + Cu2Cl2/HCl → C6H5Cl + N2. (1 mark)

(v) Side-chain chlorination in sunlight, then aqueous hydrolysis: C6H5CH3 + Cl2 → C6H5CH2Cl + HCl (hν); C6H5CH2Cl + KOH (aq) → C6H5CH2OH + KCl. (1 mark)

pyq.q: (a) Explain why the halogen atom in a haloarene is deactivating yet ortho- and para-directing in electrophilic substitution. (b) Write the equations for the nitration and the Friedel-Crafts acylation of chlorobenzene. (c) Give one use each of CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, CHCl<sub>3</sub>, CHI<sub>3</sub>, CCl<sub>4</sub> and freon 12, and one harmful effect of freons.
pyq.answer:
(a) Two opposing effects operate. The −I (inductive) effect of the electronegative halogen withdraws electron density from the ring, making it less reactive than benzene towards electrophiles: the halogen is deactivating. The +R (resonance) effect of the halogen lone pairs pushes electron density into the ring, and the resonance structures place the negative charge on the ortho and para carbons only. Attack at those positions is therefore favoured relative to the meta position, so the halogen is o/p-directing; the para product predominates because of steric hindrance at the ortho positions. (2 marks; draw the resonance structures)

(b) Nitration: C6H5Cl + HNO3 (conc. H2SO4) → 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene (major) + 1-chloro-2-nitrobenzene (minor) + H2O. Acylation: C6H5Cl + CH3COCl (anhydrous AlCl3) → 4-chloroacetophenone (major) + 2-chloroacetophenone (minor) + HCl. (1 mark)

(c) CH2Cl2: paint remover or aerosol propellant. CHCl3: solvent for fats, alkaloids and iodine; used to make the refrigerant R-22. CHI3: antiseptic (due to the iodine it liberates). CCl4: manufacture of refrigerants and propellants; cleaning fluid and fire extinguisher. Freon 12 (CCl2F2): refrigerant in refrigeration and air conditioning, aerosol propellant. Harmful effect: freons diffuse unchanged into the stratosphere and initiate radical chain reactions that deplete the ozone layer. (2 marks)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. Nucleophilic substitution in haloalkanes proceeds by two mechanisms. In the SN2 mechanism, studied by Hughes and Ingold, the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite to the leaving group in a single step; the rate depends on the concentration of both the halide and the nucleophile, and the configuration at the carbon is inverted. In the SN1 mechanism the halide first ionises slowly to a planar carbocation, which is then attacked rapidly by the nucleophile; the rate depends only on the halide, and an optically active substrate gives a racemic product. Polar protic solvents favour SN1 while polar aprotic solvents favour SN2.
(i) Write the rate law for the reaction of bromomethane with OH−.
(ii) Arrange CH3CH2Br, (CH3)2CHBr and (CH3)3CBr in increasing order of reactivity towards SN1, with reason.
(iii) (−)-2-Bromooctane reacts with aqueous NaOH to give (+)-octan-2-ol. What does this tell you about the mechanism?
(iv) Why do allyl chloride and benzyl chloride react readily by SN1 although they are primary halides?
pyq.answer:
(i) Bromomethane is a methyl halide and reacts by SN2: rate = k[CH3Br][OH−], second order. (1 mark)

(ii) CH3CH2Br < (CH3)2CHBr < (CH3)3CBr. SN1 goes through a carbocation, and carbocation stability rises from primary to secondary to tertiary because of the +I effect and hyperconjugation of alkyl groups. (1 mark)

(iii) The product has the opposite sign of rotation and the inverted configuration, so the reaction went with inversion, characteristic of SN2 backside attack; an SN1 path would have given a racemic, optically inactive mixture. (1 mark)

(iv) The carbocations they form (allyl and benzyl cations) are stabilised by resonance: the positive charge is delocalised over the C=C double bond or the benzene ring, so the slow ionisation step is easy despite the halides being primary. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. Chlorobenzene is much less reactive than chloroethane towards nucleophiles. The lone pairs on chlorine are delocalised into the ring, so the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and is shorter (169 pm) than in chloroalkanes (177 pm). Chlorobenzene is converted into phenol only by heating with aqueous NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm (Dow's process). Electron-withdrawing groups at the ortho and para positions make the substitution easier: 4-nitrochlorobenzene reacts with 15% NaOH at 443 K, 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene at 368 K, and 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene is hydrolysed by warm water. In contrast, chlorobenzene readily undergoes electrophilic substitution, the halogen directing the new group to the ortho and para positions.
(i) Draw or describe the resonance structures that explain the partial double-bond character of the C–Cl bond.
(ii) Why does a nitro group at the meta position not increase the ease of nucleophilic substitution?
(iii) Why is the phenyl cation not formed, ruling out an SN1 path?
(iv) Name the major product when chlorobenzene is treated with concentrated H2SO4.
pyq.answer:
(i) Five structures: neutral chlorobenzene, and four in which a chlorine lone pair forms a C=Cl+ double bond while a negative charge sits on an ortho carbon, the para carbon or the other ortho carbon, returning to the neutral form. The C–Cl bond is thus a hybrid of single and double bonds. (1 mark)

(ii) In the intermediate carbanion formed by nucleophilic attack, the negative charge is delocalised only over the ortho and para carbons relative to the point of attack. A nitro group at those positions can take the charge onto its oxygens and stabilise the intermediate; a meta nitro group never carries the charge in any resonance structure, so it gives no stabilisation. (1 mark)

(iii) In the phenyl cation the empty orbital lies in the plane of the ring, perpendicular to the π system, so the positive charge cannot be delocalised by resonance. The cation is highly unstable and the C–Cl bond does not ionise. (1 mark)

(iv) Sulphonation gives 4-chlorobenzenesulphonic acid as the major product (with a little of the 2-isomer), because chlorine is ortho/para-directing and the para position is less hindered. (1 mark)

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a vinylic halide?
practice_mcq.explanation: In a vinylic halide the halogen is on an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon of a C=C double bond: chloroethene. The first is allylic, the third benzylic and the fourth aryl.

practice_mcq.q: Which methyl halide has the highest dipole moment?
practice_mcq.explanation: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl (1.860 D) edges out CH<sub>3</sub>F (1.847 D) because the C–F bond is so short that its charge separation over distance is smaller despite fluorine's higher electronegativity.

practice_mcq.q: The best reagent to convert an alcohol into an alkyl chloride in pure form is
practice_mcq.explanation: With thionyl chloride the by-products SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl are gases and escape, leaving pure alkyl chloride.

practice_mcq.q: Swarts reaction is used to prepare
practice_mcq.explanation: Heating an alkyl chloride or bromide with AgF, Hg<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>, CoF<sub>2</sub> or SbF<sub>3</sub> exchanges the halogen for fluorine.

practice_mcq.q: Iodination of benzene is carried out in the presence of an oxidising agent such as HNO<sub>3</sub> because
options: The HI formed reduces the iodobenzene back to benzene
Iodine does not react with FeI<sub>3</sub>
practice_mcq.explanation: Iodination is reversible since HI is a reducing agent; the oxidising agent destroys HI and pushes the reaction forward.

practice_mcq.q: Propene reacts with HBr in the presence of benzoyl peroxide to give
practice_mcq.explanation: The peroxide effect gives anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr, placing Br on the terminal carbon.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following compounds boils highest?
practice_mcq.explanation: Boiling point rises with the number of halogen atoms because the molar mass and van der Waals forces increase, so CCl<sub>4</sub> (350 K) is highest.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following undergoes S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction fastest with aqueous KOH?
practice_mcq.explanation: S<sub>N</sub>2 needs an unhindered carbon for backside attack; reactivity is CH<sub>3</sub>X > 1° > 2° > 3°.

practice_mcq.q: Hydrolysis of an optically active 2-bromobutane by the S<sub>N</sub>1 route gives
practice_mcq.explanation: The planar carbocation is attacked from both faces with equal probability, giving equal amounts of both enantiomers, which is optically inactive.

practice_mcq.q: 2-Bromobutane heated with alcoholic KOH gives mainly
practice_mcq.explanation: Dehydrohalogenation follows Saytzeff's rule: the more substituted alkene, but-2-ene, is the major product.

practice_mcq.q: Ethyl bromide treated with KNO<sub>2</sub> gives mainly
practice_mcq.explanation: Ionic KNO<sub>2</sub> attacks through oxygen to give the alkyl nitrite C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>ONO; covalent AgNO<sub>2</sub> attacks through nitrogen to give nitroethane.

practice_mcq.q: Chlorobenzene and methyl chloride heated with sodium in dry ether give
practice_mcq.explanation: This is the Wurtz-Fittig reaction: an aryl halide and an alkyl halide couple to give an alkylarene, here methylbenzene (toluene).

practice_mcq.q: Chloroform is stored in dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim because in air and light it forms
practice_mcq.explanation: 2CHCl<sub>3</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2COCl<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl in light; phosgene is highly poisonous, so air and light are excluded.
Freon 12 is dichlorodifluoromethane, made from CCl<sub>4</sub> by the Swarts reaction and used as a refrigerant.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is hydrolysed to a phenol most easily?
practice_mcq.explanation: Three nitro groups at ortho and para positions strongly stabilise the intermediate carbanion; warm water alone hydrolyses it. A meta nitro group does not help.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following statements about a racemic mixture is correct?
options: It rotates plane-polarised light to the right
It contains equal amounts of two enantiomers and is optically inactive
It is formed only in S<sub>N</sub>2 reactions
practice_mcq.explanation: Equal amounts of the (+) and (−) forms cancel each other's rotation; such mixtures form in S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions of chiral halides.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is the correct IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH(Cl)CH(Br)CH<sub>3</sub>?
practice_mcq.explanation: Both halogens get locants 2 and 3 from either end; the tie is broken alphabetically, so bromo takes the lower number.

common_mistakes: Calling benzyl chloride an aryl halide. The chlorine is on the sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub>, so it is a benzylic (alkyl-type) halide and is highly reactive; only chlorobenzene, with Cl on the ring carbon, is an aryl halide.

Writing that CH<sub>3</sub>F has the highest dipole moment among methyl halides because fluorine is the most electronegative. NCERT's values give CH<sub>3</sub>Cl the highest (1.860 D) because the very short C–F bond reduces the charge separation.

Giving the S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2 reactivity orders the wrong way round, or forgetting that both increase from fluoride to iodide. S<sub>N</sub>2: CH<sub>3</sub>X > 1° > 2° > 3°; S<sub>N</sub>1: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH<sub>3</sub>X; leaving group RI > RBr > RCl > RF for both.

Reporting only the major alkene in a dehydrohalogenation question that asks for all products, or picking the less substituted alkene as major. Saytzeff's rule gives the more substituted alkene as the major product.
Applying the peroxide effect to HCl or HI. Only HBr adds anti-Markovnikov in the presence of peroxide; conversions such as propene to 1-bromopropane depend on this.

Mixing up the ambident nucleophile pairs: KCN gives nitriles (R–CN) and AgCN gives isocyanides (R–NC); KNO<sub>2</sub> gives alkyl nitrites (R–O–N=O) and AgNO<sub>2</sub> gives nitroalkanes (R–NO<sub>2</sub>).

Explaining the low reactivity of chlorobenzene with only one reason and no resonance structures. The scheme rewards resonance, sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation, instability of the phenyl cation and repulsion, each as a separate point.
Nitrating benzene before brominating when asked for 4-bromonitrobenzene. Nitro is meta-directing, so bromination must come first and nitration second.

Forgetting the conditions: dry ether for Grignard, Wurtz and Fittig reactions; dry acetone for Finkelstein; 273–278 K for diazotisation; 623 K and 300 atm for the Dow's process. Missing conditions cost half a mark each.
strategy:
Treat this chapter as the foundation of the organic unit rather than as six marks on its own: half of what you learn here (alcoholic versus aqueous KOH, KCN versus AgCN, Sandmeyer, Grignard, the peroxide effect) reappears in Alcohols, Aldehydes and Amines conversions. Start with classification and nomenclature in one sitting, doing NCERT 6.1, 6.2 and 6.3 completely because the board sets those exact structures.

Then spend your longest sitting on section 6.7.1. Write the SN2 and SN1 mechanisms from memory, with the transition state, the carbocation and the stereochemical result, until each takes under four minutes. Attach to them the two reactivity orders, the leaving-group order, and the three chirality examples (2-bromobutane, butan-2-ol, bromochloroiodomethane). Next learn the chlorobenzene story as one drawing: the five resonance structures answer the low reactivity question, the o/p-direction question and the shorter C–Cl bond question.

Memorise: the name reactions with reagents and conditions (Sandmeyer, Finkelstein, Swarts, Wurtz, Wurtz-Fittig, Fittig, Dow's process), the give-reason answers in sections 6.3, 6.4 and 6.6, the four conditions for hydrolysis of nitrochlorobenzenes, and one use plus one harmful effect for each polyhalogen compound. Derive rather than memorise: dehydrohalogenation products by Saytzeff's rule, and the products of any nucleophile from the table in 6.7.1.

In the last two days do NCERT 6.10, 6.11, 6.14, 6.16, 6.19, 6.21 and 6.22 on paper. In the exam, give conditions over every arrow, name the mechanism when you write one, and for give-reason questions write the two marking phrases the examiner is looking for rather than a paragraph.
